label: text
text: Definite signs are forthcoming that the authorities in Canton are taking steps to restrain the alleged ex-seamen who are picketing the Sheamboat Co's wharves. Further improvement in traffic and trade has been noticed since the end of last week.

label: text
text: A merchant who made the round-trip by the s.s. "Taishan" stressed Canton police patrols demonstrating with the "plain-shes pickets who were directing passengers to the other steam-oats, but no arrest was made. Mr. T. V. Soong, Minister of finance in the Nationalist Gov-

label: text

label: paragraph_title
text: EXCELLENT NEWS

label: paragraph_title
text: Wuchow "Wonders" if Boycott Existed".

label: text
text: According to our informant, all ships are carrying bumper cargoes both ways—a striking contrast to the state of affairs on the Kong-moon run. The same applied to passenger traffic.

label: text
text: Interviewed by the "China "China Mail," a passenger who returned to the Colony by the s.s. "Tai Ming" yesterday afternoon, stated that conditions on the West River were gradually returning to normal. "Were it not for the carryings on at Do-sing, one would wonder whether it was true that there had ever been such a thing as a boycott."

label: text
text: "On arrival at Wuchow, we were agreeably surprised to find that the Chamber of Commerce had posted up notices or proclamations stating that foreign cargo was in no way to be inter-forced with."

label: paragraph_title
text: Free British Entry.

label: text
text: All British goods have free entry now and our cargo went straight on to the "Pai" (the ponoon jetty).

label: text
text: "At the Cliff—near Kamchuk—we leave the Kongmoon ships and get going at full speed, arriving at Samshui at about 10 a.m. We remain there, as formerly, until the arrival of the train from Canton. There is no escort from the Cliff, but gunboats are noticed at intervals as far as Samshui."

label: text
text: "The old routine is now observed. We leave here at 5.30 p.m. All Kongmoon and Wuchow shipe of that day assemble at Wangmoon early the following morning and proceed upwards accompanied by a gunboat—speed regulated to suit the slowest ship."

label: paragraph_title
text: Mineral Water Protest.

label: text
text: “The searchers appeared somewhat disgusted at finding no opium and wanted to seize our mineral waters — British, of course. They made quite a scene, sending for their chief who said that they should have been stamped by the Nationalist Government. Our captain explained that they were merely for the ship's consumption and there was no further trouble:

label: text
text: "At Shiuhing we remain just as long as is necessary to discharge our cargo. Taking is of little importance and the same could be said as regards Do-sing were it not for the opium search. This time we were only visited by two individuals."

label: text
text: "We brought back with us a full cargo, also 120 head of cattle and a number of pigs and chick-eng. There is an abundance of livestock on the beach at Wuchow and prices in Hong Kong should come down."

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text:
MISCONDUCT BY CHINESE
CONSTABLE.

label: paragraph_title
text: MAGISTRATE'S REBEUKE.

label: text
text: Chinese "constable" No. C 392, stationed at Pokfulam "Police Station, was "the defendant in an opium case heard by Mr. R. E. Lindsell at the Central Magistracy this morning.

label: text
text: Witness informed the Sikh sergeant on duty at the time and the latter, accompanied by the witness and P.C.C. 161, entered the sleeping quarters and proceeded to search the accused's belongings.

label: text
text: According to the evidence of P.C.C. 223, accused was been to enter his sleeping quarters at 8.45 p.m. on Saturday evening, remove two tins of opium from his jacket and place same in his locker.

label: text
text: Acquired snatched up the jacket and ran out of the door. One tin fell out of the jacket pocket.

label: text
text: This the defendant picked up and threw away. Both tins were subsequently found in the bushes.

label: text
text: "Accused," who was not represented by counsel, denied the charge, adding that he knew the regulations regarding opinion and that he had never possessed even the smallest quantity of the forbidden drug.

label: paragraph_title
text: Been Telling Lies.

label: text
text: Mr. Lindsell: There may be something in that, but are you asking me to believe such an extraordinary thing as this: that

label: text
text: police officers going out to search for something they saw you throw away, find two tins of opium—opium in the jungle?

label: text
text:
His Worship: Do you mean to suggest that all these witnesses have been telling lies in order to send you to jail?—Yes.
Mr. Lindsell: Oh, I see. But can you explain why? There had been a quarrel on the previous Friday. It was over the question of cleaning the revolvers in Monday mornings.

label: paragraph_title
text: Wanted a Solicitor.

label: text
text: The accused maintained his denial, protesting that the story had been fabricated.

label: text
text: "I do not believe a word of your story," continued Mr. Lind sell. "You are convicted."

label: text
text: Accused: I wish to have this case reminded in order that I may instruct a solicitor. It is entirely false.

label: text
text: His Worship, in refusing the application for a remand, said that he was quite satisfied with the evidence, which was corroborative in every respect. Defendant would be fined $1,000 or six months.

label: text
text: 'DARTMOUTH' FIRE ON WAY

label: text
text: THREATENED AMMUNION?

label: text
text:
Although official confirmation is not forthcoming of facts other than that there was a fire aboard H.M.S. "Dartmouth" on her way out to Hong Kong (the cruiser arrived in Hong Kong on Friday), one report has it that it occurred when the vessel was between Gibraltar and Malta and that it involved the fuel tanks.
It is also stated that there was a possibility for a few days after the outbreak of the fire assuming a serious aspect and that in consequence it was found necessary to move stores and ammunition.
H.M.S. "Dartmouth" has about 400 men on board. It is reported that two men on board died from natural causes during the trip out to Hong Kong; one of these is said to have been a stoker and the other a canteen manager.

label: paragraph_title
text: Opinion

label: paragraph_title
text: EXCEPT ON FACTS

label: paragraph_title
text: Alleged Spiritualist Loses Her

label: text
text: The case in which evidence figured as to "magic ten" propitiatory to the "spirits" and an alleged midnight scene in the course of which it is alleged that a spirit took promotion of a woman dictating to the later of the house in which she should male a woman in question, came to a conclusion this morning, final evidence being given and judgment entered.

label: text
text: Mr. M. K. Lo addressed the court for the defendant (a Chinese na-countant who was alleged to have given the woman plaintiff $1,000 as a wedding dowry and then to have taken it to seek as a loan and not repaid it.)

label: text
text: The plaintiff, who was the former wife of the defendant, claimed for the return of the $1,000 and it was alleged against her by the defence that she had by pretence to supernatural powers, intimidated the defendant into marrying her. It was also alleged that she received the $1,000 marriage dowry and kept a promissory note for its payment on which she was suing.

label: paragraph_title
text: A "Pai Sun Poh."

label: text
text: Mr. Lo, addressing the court said that the only question in the case was as to whether or not the plaintiff did pay to the defendant the sum of $1,000 under an acknowledgment note as a loan, having already received it as a wedding dowry. This was denied by the defence which had put up a different story and he (Mr. Lo) submitted that the evidence bore out the defendant's story and that the plaintiff had failed to prove the alleged repayment in the form of a loan.

label: text
text: Mr. Lo asked His Honour to consider who and what the plaintiff was. As against her story as to being engaged in the harmless and innocuous occupation of a herbalist he submitted that from the evidence of the defendants His Honour could not but come irresistibly to the conclusion that she had held herself out to be something more than an ordinary person. The evidence pointed conclusively to her having held herself out to be a "pul sun poh" (one practising in the supernatural).

label: text
text: Mr. Lo, dealing with the evidence called for the plaintiffs submitted that certain matters went to prove that the statements made as to the money having been paid over by the plaintiff to the defendant were rehearsed. In support of this, he drew attention to the fact that certain of the witnesses were relatives of the plaintiff and referred to the evidence of the servant girl. Was it likely, he asked, that her mistress would have taken a servant girl so fully into her confidence as to explain that her husband or his firm was in financial difficulties and that she was lending him to tide over bad times the very money he had paid as a marriage dowry?

label: text
text:
"Unadulterated Perjury."
Dealing with the denial of the plaintiff that she had pretended to supernatural powers by which she had influenced the defendant and the "kit fat" wife she had replaced, Mr. Lo said that it was unadulterated perjury. He submitted that the evidence of the Chinese reporter who called at the house and wrote a report in the Chinese press went to show this. As an unbiased witness, merely recording something unusual, in that a young man, already with a "kit fat" wife, was taking to himself a woman many years his senior, the reporter had correctly reported the facts of the case, said Mr. Lo. The report clearly proved that the woman had claimed to exercise supernatural powers.

label: text
text: Mr. Lo termed her an "idiotic story" the plaintiff's contention that the defendant and his former "kit fat" wife had conspired to a fendish and diabolic plot against her and that it was subsequent to this that the defendant and his former "kit fat" wife had prevailed on her to marry the defendant. Mr. Lo said that the defendant would have had to have been a "senior wrangler in rasseldom" to have conceived the plot and to have fabricated the subsequent story as the plaintiff alleged.
